Last spring, just prior to the end of the academic year at the University OwHe was
privileged to attend, he had occasion to take part in a meeting of his Chapter of Psi
Upsilon. The meeting was conducted with all the solemnity and decorum of years past.
At the close all present formed an unbroken circle, clasped hands as Brothers have
done from time immemorial, and raised their voices in "Dear Old Shrine." It was a
moment to be remembered. The words still are ringing in my ears.
"We love thee yet, we'll ne'er forget the days of auld lang syne." You remember. Or,
if you don't, they may be found in "Songs of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity"�
the last
phrases of the beautiful refrain which follows each of the three beckoning verses. In
those few words may be found the true mysticism which has made Psi Upsilon what
it is. They tie the present with the past. They make us one.
Shifting the scene, Owlie recently had the pleasure of reviewing the record totals of
the Annual Giving Program for 1975-76. What a lift to find that so many more of the
Brethren than the year before had come forward to give what they could and thereby
swell the amount contributed from less than $37,000 to more than $50,000! Owlie is
not long on statistics, but apparently nearly two hundred rallied to the cause who have
never given before, and the honor roll of contributors jumped from under fourteen
hundred Psi U's to over eighteen hundred! This augurs weU for the future.
These two seemingly unrelated accounts may appear to be a strange introduction
for this editorial. If you will think about it, however, you will realize that there is a
very obvious relationship. At some time in the past each of us learned to add our voices
to the chorus, "We love thee yet, we'll ne'er forget the days of auld lang syne." It
truly can be said that the many who have participated in the Annual Giving Program
year after year "love thee yet," Psi Upsilon, have not forgotten, and will "ne'er for
get." Now a goodly number of additional voices have joined in the chorus of partici
pation. These, too, love her yet and will not forget. As the third verse of this same
hallowed song recites, "linked by a chain" does have real and tangible significance.
At the same time there remain upwards of fifteen thousand Brothers who are not yet
aware of this relationship between the Shrine Song and the Annual Giving Program.

poses our Brothers to many stresses and pressures. It is wholly understandable that so

The 133rd Convention a Business and Social Success;
The Omicron Chapter Proves to Be a Genial Host

As one hundred and forty-eight loyal alumni, under
graduates, wives, and dates joined in a giant circle
with clasped hands at the Round Barn in Champaign,
Illinois on Saturday evening, August twenty-eighth,
for the traditional singing of "Dear Old Shrine," the
133rd Convention of Psi Upsilon drew to a fitting
close. This was the final scene at the Convention Ban
quet, which climaxed four days of productive meet
ings and enlivening social activities.
Earlier in the evening the guests had been treated
to a magnificent dinner under the supervision of
R. Kevin Graham, Omicron '73, able manager of this
large and popular eating facility. Robert R. Pfeiffer,
Omicron '62 had capably filled the role of toastmaster
and had introduced, among others, Guy C. Fraker,
III '60, Omicron's Alumni President, and Thomas W.
McCaffer, Jr., Omicron '77, Undergraduate President.
Robert W. Morey, Pi '20, President of the Executive
Council, had presented the trophy for academic dis
tinction in 1975-76 to the Theta Theta Chapter. And
E. Willis Brown, Omicron-Mu '31, a noted journaHst,
had delivered the principal address of the evening,
touching nostalgically on our great heritage in Psi
Upsilon and the justifiable pride we may take in our
fraternal ties.
On Wednesday, the twenty-fotnth, undergraduate
delegates from twenty-two Chapters had converged
on the University of Illinois for three simultaneous
Regional Mini-Conferences. These provided a wel
come opportunity for members from the same geo
graphical area to become acquainted, compare notes,
and share both successes and concerns. Meetings that
first day and throughout the balance of the week, as
well as dinners and all rooming accommodations, were
centered in the twenty-one floor Century Twentyone,
a modem hotel just three blocks from the Omicron
Chapter House.
Robert W. Morey, Pi '20 leads singing, flanked by
Frederick A. Nichols, Omicron '28, Guy C. Fraker, III,
Omicron '60, and Joseph A. Esquirol, Delta '17.
The Convention opened formally the next afternoon,
with Brother Morey reciting the traditional opening
words spoken at all Chapter meetings of the Pi. So
ambitious was the agenda considered by the seven
standing committees during the succeeding two days
that planned workshops for specific areas of responsi
bility in operating a Chapter gave way to extra com
mittee and general meetings. The atmosphere through
out was one of serious apphcation, determined prog
ress, and constructive spirit.
Among the principal actions taken was the raising
of annual Chapter taxes from $20 to $25 for each
member and an increase of the initial payment from
$20 for a lifetime Diamond subscription to $30, now
to be called an initiation fee and still including $20
for the Diamond lifetime subscription. Deeply im
pressed by the extraordinary growth of the Annual
Giving Program through more and larger alumni con
tributions, the undergraduate delegates felt that stu
dent members must respond comparably in order to
balance the Fraternity's operating budget.

Thmrsday. "It's time

indicate that their affiliation with us ended when they
left the college or university campus. . . . You under

this project, as well as pledge your continuing support
and interest when you terminate your undergraduate
careers ... I ask that each of you . . . take this mes

join a crusade to re-establish viable alumni con
Other memorable features were an
outstanding
presentation of rushing procedures and techniques
by three Epsilon Omega undergraduates and an actual
initiation ceremony performed by the Omicron Chap
ter. Delegates attended as observers the summer meet
ing of the Executive Council on Thursday evening
and were treated to a street dance Friday evening,
a popular function at the University of Illinois with
all the students back on campus for registration. The
tapping of beer kegs at the Chapter House every eve
ning typified the convivial hospitahty extended by the
Omicron throughout the four-day period.
Judging by the delegates and other members who
attended the 133rd Convention, all Chapters are to
be commended for sustaining the Fraternity's historic
standard of selecting for membership young men of
character, will, determination, and a keen under
standing of what it means to be a Psi U.
A vast amount of credit must be given to the com
